The study uses terahertz near-field imaging to investigate electromagnetic coupling in SRR metamaterial arrays.
Two coupling regimes are identified: near-field coupling at small lattice periodicities and far-field diffractive coupling at larger periodicities.
SRR arrays were fabricated with copper structures 10 µm thick on 120 µm PTFE substrates.
Lattice periodicities were varied from 380 µm to 1200 µm in x and y directions.
Near-field mapping was performed with spatial resolution of about 30 µm (~λ/20 at 0.5 THz).
The fundamental plasmonic resonance (n=1) occurs near 162 GHz, corresponding to a magnetic dipole (LC) mode.
A higher-order plasmonic resonance (n=3) near 400 GHz corresponds to an electric quadrupole mode.
Near-field coupling causes spectral broadening and reduced Q-factors, especially for the n=1 mode.
Electric near-fields transition from circular to linearly polarized with decreasing lattice spacing for the n=1 mode.
Magnetic near-fields compress spatially with decreasing spacing for the n=3 mode, maintaining quadrupolar structure.
Diffractive coupling occurs when lattice periodicity matches the resonance wavelength, enabling radiative coupling.
Far-field transmission spectra show sharp features associated with lattice modes (1,0) and (0,1) diffraction orders.
Q-factors increase with lattice periodicity, more strongly for the n=3 mode than for the n=1 mode.
Finite Element Method simulations reproduce near-field patterns of single SRRs, validating experimental data.
Near-field maps reveal hybridization of plasmonic and lattice modes in the diffractive coupling regime.
Superradiant decay of collective modes leads to spectral broadening in dense SRR arrays.
The near-field probe detects both in-plane electric fields and out-of-plane magnetic fields using Faraday’s law.
The effective refractive index used for resonance frequency estimation is approximately 1.2, between PTFE and air.
The study extends previous far-field transmission studies by providing near-field electromagnetic maps.
The near-field detector is separated from the sample by a ~40 µm dielectric protective layer with refractive index 1.5.
